Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission. The 2010 Supreme Court decision that held restrictions on independent campaign spending by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment. Citizens United, a nonprofit corporation, sought to air a film criticizing Hillary Clinton during the 2008 primary. McCain-Feingold campaign finance restrictions blocked the film. The organization challenged the law's ban on corporate and union independent expenditures as a violation of free speech.

Justice John Roberts' majority held that political speech by corporations is protected and cannot be limited based on the speaker's corporate status. The Court treated corporate spending as a form of political speech entitled to First Amendment protection, equating money with speech. This struck down decades of campaign finance regulation. Corporations and unions could now spend unlimited sums independently in elections. The decision overturned portions of McCain-Feingold and earlier precedent, Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce, unleashing record campaign spending. The ruling fundamentally transformed American election funding and regulation by extending free speech protection to corporate campaign spending.
